catalog_quote: [Smyth 1920] 149. There are three accents in Greek. No Greek accent can stand farther back than the antepenult. ... 151. Accented syllables in Ancient Greek had a higher pitch ... than unaccented syllables, and it was the rising and falling of the pitch that made Ancient Greek a musical language. ... Musical accent (elevation and depression of tone) is to be distinguished from quantity (duration of tone), and from rhythmic accent (stress of voice at fixed intervals when there is a regular sequence of long and short syllables). ... 159. An accent is called recessive when it moves back as far from the end of the word as the quantity of the ultima permits (166). ... 162. audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every clause of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the two held scanned texts at the stated sections/pages (Smyth pp. 37-39, Buck p. 79). The classification tonal-OR-pitch accent for the Aeolic/Doric/NW Greek node rests on a standard reference grammar (Smyth 1920) plus the standard dialect handbook (Buck 1910), and I downloaded Buck's own 1955 revision (The Greek Dialects, section 103, p. 85), which repeats the dialect-accent statement nearly word for word -- so the dialectological content is not an artefact of an outdated edition.
